title: Short or long (Berakhot 34a)
hook: one student prays long, another short; Rabbi Eliezer says Moses did both
tomorrow: how could a sage tell his prayer for the sick got through?

segments.voice: Yesterday: everything is in heaven's hands except the fear of heaven, and awe is the big vessel only Moses found small. Today, Moses again, praying two very different ways.
screen: `AWE IS YOURS TO CHOOSE.` → `MOSES, TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: A hospital waiting room, early morning. One relative has a book of psalms open and plans to read for an hour. Another says one sentence, quietly, and puts her coffee down. A third person is annoyed with both of them. So which does a scared family need, the long prayer or the short one? The Talmud has a scene with exactly this argument in it, and it refuses to pick a side.
screen: `A BOOK OF PSALMS, AN HOUR.` → `ONE QUIET SENTENCE.` → `WHICH ONE?`

segments.voice: A student goes up to lead the prayer in front of Rabbi Eliezer, and he goes long. Really long. The other students mutter: how drawn out he is. Rabbi Eliezer says: is he longer than Moses? Moses lay before God forty days and forty nights, pleading for his people. Then another student leads, and he's quick. The students mutter again: how short he is. Rabbi Eliezer says: is he shorter than Moses? When his sister Miriam was struck ill, Moses prayed in one breath: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." Here are the two views, at their best. The long camp: some things need staying. A people's whole future, a grief, a fear that doesn't fit in a sentence. Leaving early can be its own kind of leaving. The short camp: when someone you love is sick in front of you, a long speech can be about you. Moses didn't make a speech for Miriam; he asked, plainly, and stopped. Rabbi Eliezer doesn't call either student wrong. He holds up one teacher who did both, at different moments. So the question was never long or short. It's what this moment is asking for.
screen: `HOW LONG HE IS!` · `FORTY DAYS, LIKE MOSES.` · `HOW SHORT HE IS!` · `HEAL HER NOW, LIKE MOSES.` · then, large: `SHORT OR LONG, AS NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind who needs something right now. Ask what this moment needs: one plain sentence for them, said out loud and left alone, or the whole sit spent holding them in mind. Do whichever it is, and don't apologize for the length.
screen: `ONE PERSON.` · `ONE SENTENCE, OR THE WHOLE SIT?` · `DO WHAT IT NEEDS.`

segments.voice: Short or long. Rabbi Eliezer's answer to both complaints: Moses prayed forty days, and Moses prayed one line.
For the pocket: short or long, as needed, the way Moses had both in him. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Jewish practice, prayers for the sick range from Moses' few words for Miriam to reading many psalms together; communities also say the Mi Shebeirach, a prayer for healing, naming the sick person.

match.prompt: two complaints, two answers — tap the pairs.
pairs: shorter than Moses? heal her now

fork.setup: a friend's dad is in the ER. in the group chat, one person wants to plan a long candle vigil tonight; another says just send her one line. what would Rabbi Eliezer say?
options: go long: a big vigil shows how much everyone cares.
go short: long gestures are always about the people giving them.
ask what she needs right now; Moses did both, at different moments.
fork.reveal: Rabbi Eliezer doesn't rule for one length. he points at Moses, who prayed forty days for his people and one line for his sick sister.

original.note: Hebrew: Numbers 12:13, Moses' prayer for Miriam: heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.

trapdoor: what you thought: real prayer is long, or real prayer is short.
what it means: both lengths are Moses' lengths; the moment decides.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 34a sets Deuteronomy's forty days and nights against Numbers 12:13's one line for Miriam, so Rabbi Eliezer answers both complaints.
guess: a prayer's length should fit what the moment is asking
long prayers count more, the way Moses prayed forty days
keep prayers brief, since God already knows what you mean
recall: awe: the one thing heaven leaves to you
a snake at the heel doesn't break prayer

chat.says: waiting room. saba's shul friend wants an hour of psalms. mom says one line is enough. who's right
options: Maybe both. Rabbi Eliezer pointed to Moses for each: long, short, as needed.
The psalms. The Talmud says the longer a prayer is, the more it counts.
Your mom. The Talmud makes fun of the student who prayed for too long.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Eliezer answers both complaints with Moses: forty days for his people, one line for Miriam. Length follows the moment.

Rabbi Eliezer.meaning: the sage who defends both the long and the short prayer

Miriam.meaning: Moses' sister; he prayed one line when she fell ill

psalms.meaning: the Bible's book of songs and prayers, Tehillim

Talmud.meaning: the sages' long discussion of Jewish law and story
